routes.description: Establish an early apostolic resurrection claim through historically trustworthy sources, then compare explanations of the reported encounters and related evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The cumulative documentary evidence must support apostolic provenance and reported encounters strongly enough that resurrection explains the record better than legend, sincere error, or deception.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative historical record provides strong evidence that Jesus rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Connect the resurrection proclamation and encounter reports to the original apostles rather than later legendary development.
Establish sufficient historical trustworthiness and informed proximity for the documentary sources carrying the reports.
Show that legend, sincere perceptual error, and deliberate deception explain the reported evidence less adequately than resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify mutually supporting source streams and cross-checkable details that contribute to the cumulative documentary case.
Explain how sufficiently strong cumulative evidence could overcome the low prior probability assigned to a resurrection.

routes.description: Require independently assessable and consistently applied support for the resurrection claim, then show that the surviving reports remain indirect, disputed, and insufficiently testable.
routes.successCriteria: The record must remain too weakly sourced, corroborated, or causally connected to establish resurrection under a standard that also discriminates among comparable supernatural claims.

motionBridge.description: Show that the surviving Christian reports do not constitute strong historical evidence establishing a resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Show that the reports lack sufficient provenance, examination, physical corroboration, or other means of independent historical testing.
Show that the reported claims do not warrant treating the narrated events as established facts requiring a supernatural explanation.
Require an evidential method that distinguishes the Christian reports from comparable rejected miracle testimony without special pleading.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Apply background knowledge and prior probability when comparing resurrection with ordinary error, transmission, or fabrication.
Account for agreement or narrative detail through shared tradition, literary dependence, or storytelling rather than historicity alone.

sectionSelections.title: Apostolic provenance and transmission
sectionSelections.rationale: Whether the resurrection claim reaches original apostolic witnesses or only later and indirect narrators determines what historical event the surviving documents can support.

proSelections.proposition: Paul's early resurrection tradition and agreement with Peter, James, and the Twelve place the resurrection proclamation with the original apostles.
Luke's access to Paul and Jerusalem leaders, together with features of the Acts travel narrative, supports Acts as an informed report of apostolic resurrection preaching.

conSelections.proposition: The biblical reports lack secure custody, examinable testimony, known provenance, and physical corroboration, leaving their resurrection claims inadequately testable.
Paul was not an eyewitness to Jesus's life or death, Luke's alleged witnesses cannot be examined, and the claimed Johannine attribution remains unverifiable.

sectionSelections.title: Documentary reliability and corroboration
sectionSelections.rationale: The inference from surviving writings to otherwise uncheckable resurrection assertions depends on whether ordinary historical accuracy and interlocking details justify broader trust.

proSelections.proposition: Numerous historical confirmations and undesigned interconnections among the Gospels and Acts cumulatively support their substantial trustworthiness and informed proximity to events.
Gospel reliability rests on accuracy in cross-checkable matters rather than authorial self-attestation, providing defeasible reason for trust in matters that cannot be checked directly.

conSelections.proposition: Shared or compatible mundane details may result from circulating stories or literary dependence and do not validate extraordinary resurrection assertions.
Although extra-biblical support was repeatedly invoked, the resurrection case presented did not supply a genuinely extra-biblical component.

sectionSelections.title: Legend, mistake, and deception
sectionSelections.rationale: The resurrection inference turns on whether the reported encounters and claimant behavior materially exclude legendary development, sincere error, or deliberate fabrication.

proSelections.proposition: The reported appearances were collective, multisensory, conversational, physical, and extended over time, making sincere perceptual error an inadequate explanation.
The apostles' willingness to suffer and die, together with the reported transformations of James and Peter, counts against deliberate fabrication.

conSelections.proposition: Legend allows the narrated events themselves to be unwarranted, while sincere belief and martyrdom cannot validate them because people sincerely accept many false claims.
A naturally possible extraordinary event is antecedently more plausible than a violation of known natural regularities, and no resurrection has been independently and scientifically verified.

sectionSelections.title: Strength, testimony, and prior probability
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion requires a standard for when documentary testimony becomes strong evidence and whether cumulative support can overcome the low prior probability of resurrection.

proSelections.proposition: Documentary evidence can be strong when multiple mutually corroborating sources converge, and the cumulative record supports reported appearances and an empty tomb.
A miraculous claim properly receives a low prior probability, but sufficiently strong cumulative documentary evidence can in principle overcome even an extremely small prior.

conSelections.proposition: Strong historical support should satisfy demanding criteria, including physical corroboration and identifiable witnesses whose testimony can be evaluated.

A report may be a data point without sufficiently supporting its proposition; credibility and background facts can support ordinary testimony, but multiplying extraordinary claims does not establish resurrection.

sectionSelections.title: Comparative consistency and cumulative inference
sectionSelections.rationale: A burden-relevant method must explain how source-specific criteria distinguish the resurrection reports from rival miracle traditions and how multiple evidential lines combine.

proSelections.proposition: Extraordinary reports should be evaluated through witness reliability, incentives to lie, possibilities of honest mistake, and relevant prior probabilities rather than rejected by category alone.
Multiple positive evidential lines cumulatively reduce the probability of myth, conspiracy, and hallucination alternatives, thereby increasing support for resurrection.

conSelections.proposition: If the evidential standard used for biblical resurrection reports would also require acceptance of analogous religious claims, that parity undermines the standard.
Having more reports for Jesus than for a weaker rival claim does not establish that the evidence is sufficient to justify belief in resurrection.
